supports.where: The sheet's title, before the words Safety Data Sheet. Section 3 lists five components: ethyl alcohol at 80-86%, isopropyl alcohol at 9%, methyl alcohol at 4-5%, methyl isobutyl ketone at 1% and water at 5%; it does not say on what basis the percentages are. The foot of the page lists the supplier's product of 95% ethyl alcohol beside this sheet. The supplier's list has no sheet for ethanol and water alone at this strength: its others are for a specially denatured alcohol and for solutions of 70% and under. So the heading over the statements says that they are those of the denatured product.
Under the title, after the words Revision Date, and again at the foot of the sheet: the revision that was read. The sheet does not say which rule its classification is made under.
Under the title, after the words Signal Word. The sheet prints it in capitals; the record stores Danger, the form its schema has for the word.
Section 2, the first hazard class it lists: flammable liquids, category 2. The record stores the line of the sheet with its code in front, then a colon and the statement.
Section 2, the second class: acute toxicity by mouth, category 4.

supports.prints: Causes skin and serious eye irritation (H315+H319)
supports.where: Section 2, the third class, for the skin and the eyes, categories 2 and 2A: the sheet joins the two codes under one statement, and the record stores them so.
Section 2, the fourth class: a single exposure, irritation of the airways, category 3.

Section 2, the fifth class: a single exposure, category 1. The line after it says that the denaturant makes the product poisonous and that it cannot be made safe to drink; the note says that the product is poisonous for what is added to it. Ethanol and water alone would not carry this statement by this sheet; the lab shows it because it cannot know which product a laboratory has.

supports.prints: Keep away from heat, sparks, open flames, and hot surfaces. No smoking (P210).
supports.where: Section 2, after the first statement. Section 10 lists what the liquid is kept from, oxidizing agents and acids among them, with heat and any source of ignition. Section 8 calls for gloves, protective clothing and eye protection, with the code P280, and for use only in a hood or where the air is changed well, with P271. Section 5 gives the flash point as 21 °C.

The heading of section 13. Under it the sheet says that the federal, state and local rules that may apply are to be looked at first, and that one of the supplier's own numbered methods is one option. The note gives no method of disposal, this one or another: it says that disposal is decided by the laboratory's own rules and local regulations.

Read and not carried. The heading of section 4. Under it, for the eyes: they are rinsed with water for several minutes, with contact lenses taken out, and medical advice is got if the irritation lasts; for skin or hair, the clothing is taken off at once and the skin rinsed. Why: NOAA's record asks for more for the eyes and says why wet clothing comes off, and the note gives its lines.

supports.prints: Liver damage, reproductive, teratogenic effects, carcinogen.
supports.where: Read and not carried. Section 11, after the label for chronic effects. Why: section 2 of the same sheet gives the product no hazard class for any of these, so the sheet does not bear its own line out; they are the effects of drinking alcohol over years, which is no part of work at a bench.

supports.where: The page's title, under the words Chemical Datasheet: a record of ethanol itself, not of a denatured product or of a solution. The page was found in the list of names the site shows under one letter; the site's search was not used, which its robots file closes to automated readers. The foot of the page prints the version named in the citation and no date of its own.

The field General Description, its last sentence. The field Fire Hazard, which the page credits to a coast guard manual of 1999, says that the liquid is flammable, that fire may flash back along a trail of vapour, and that the vapour may explode if it is lit in a closed space. The note says that a flame can run back along the vapour.

The name of the field, a text the page credits to a pocket guide of a federal institute, 2024. It has work clothing that gets wet taken off at once, and gives the reason in brackets: that the liquid is flammable. It asks for clothing that keeps the liquid from the skin and for protection for the eyes.

The name of the field, a text the page credits to a toxicology programme, 1992. For the eyes: contact lenses are looked for and taken out, the eyes are flushed with water or salt solution for 20 to 30 minutes while a hospital or a poison centre is called, and the person is taken to a hospital after, whether or not anything shows. The supplier's sheet gives several minutes; the note gives this as what the lab goes by.

Read and not carried. The name of the field, a long list of what ethanol reacts with violently: some acid chlorides, concentrated sulfuric acid with strong hydrogen peroxide, hypochlorous acid and chlorine, potassium, and others. Why: none of them is on this bench, and the supplier's sheet already keeps the liquid from oxidizers and acids, which the note says.

Read and not carried. The name of the field, a text from a guide for emergencies of 2024 for flammable liquids that mix with water: sources of ignition are removed, and a spill is kept out of waterways and sewers. Why: it is the guide's standing text for a class of liquids and a spill from a tank; no document read gives ethanol a class for the environment.
